summary: Defines the Static Context Header Compression and fragmentation framework, designed for Low-Power Wide Area Networks. Compression relies on a static context kept both on the device and in the network, and the document gives a generic mechanism and its use for IPv6 and UDP headers, plus optional fragmentation.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny devices can send very little. If both sides keep the same codebook, a long header can shrink to a short code word.

questions: how does schc compress ipv6 and udp headers
what are the schc fragmentation modes
subtitle: How tiny, battery-powered devices shrink IPv6 and UDP headers to a rule number, and split big packets into tiles, without any sync traffic.

tldr.problem: Low-Power Wide Area Networks carry very small frames, devices sleep most of the time, and the return path may be costly or missing, yet IPv6 and UDP headers are large and IPv6 expects a 1280-byte MTU.
tldr.mechanism: Both ends hold the same static Context of Rules. The sender replaces known header fields with a short RuleID plus a residue of the bits that vary, and an optional fragmentation layer cuts the result into tiles with three reliability modes.
tldr.outcome: A whole IPv6/UDP header can often shrink to little more than a RuleID. Technology-specific choices are left to Profiles, and the RFC has since been updated by RFC 9441.

today: RFC 8724 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2020, and it is updated by RFC 9441. It is a generic framework: the RFC leaves technology-specific settings to Profiles specified in other documents.

sections.title: The LPWAN Problem
sections.content:
RFC 8724 defines Static Context Header Compression and fragmentation (SCHC), pronounced like sheek. It was designed for Low-Power Wide Area Networks (LPWANs), where devices sleep most of the time, may only receive for short periods after they transmit, and send greatly reduced data units.

The RFC points out two properties it can exploit. The topology is a star, so all packets between the same source and destination follow the same path. And devices embed built-in applications, so the traffic to compress is known in advance.

The Context is static: the field values and the actions to compress them do not change over time. That avoids resynchronization, which matters because a return path may be more restricted or expensive, or sometimes completely unavailable. A compression protocol that relies on feedback does not fit such networks.

SCHC also offers an optional fragmentation and reassembly mechanism, because some LPWAN technologies lack their own and IPv6 requires an MTU of 1280 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny sensors in the middle of a field can only whisper short messages and sleep a lot. So the two sides agree on a shared codebook ahead of time and never need to chat to keep it up to date.

sections.title: Where SCHC Sits
sections.content:
SCHC is an adaptation layer between an upper layer such as IPv6 and an underlying LPWAN technology. It has two sublayers: Compression on top and Fragmentation below it. Compression is always attempted first. The result is called a SCHC Packet whether or not anything was actually compressed, and fragmentation is applied only if the underlying layer needs it. The decision not to fragment is left to each Profile.

The RFC uses the vocabulary of RFC 8376: Devices (Dev), the Radio Gateway (RGW), the Network Gateway (NGW) and the Application Server (App). The SCHC compressor/decompressor (C/D) and fragmenter/reassembler (F/R) sit on both sides of the LPWAN link, on the Dev and on the network infrastructure side. On the network side they can be part of the NGW or located in the Internet as long as a tunnel is established between them and the NGW. Both sides MUST share the same set of Rules.

A SCHC Packet is the Compressed Header followed by the original payload. The Compressed Header is a RuleID plus a Compression Residue, which may be empty. Both can have variable size and need not be a multiple of bytes.

A Profile is a particular setting of all the SCHC parameters, listed in Appendix D of the RFC. Both ends must be provisioned with the same Profile and the same Rules before they communicate. Data models for Contexts and Profiles are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a post office that first squeezes your letter into a tiny note, then, if the envelope is still too big, cuts it into postcards. The post office at the other end glues everything back and expands it.

sections.title: Rules and Field Descriptors
sections.content:
The Context is a set of Rules. Each Rule is identified by a RuleID and holds a list of Field Descriptors, listed in the order the fields appear in the packet header. A RuleID has meaning only for one Dev, so different Devs can reuse the same RuleID for different Rules. Compression Rules and fragmentation Rules share one RuleID space. The RuleID size is not fixed by the RFC; Profiles define it. At least one RuleID MUST be allocated to tagging packets for which no compression Rule matched.

A Field Descriptor has seven entries: Field ID (FID), Field Length (FL), Field Position (FP), Direction Indicator (DI), Target Value (TV), Matching Operator (MO) and Compression/Decompression Action (CDA). The DI can be Up, Dw or Bi. An FP of 1 means the first occurrence of a field, and 0 means don't care.

To compress a packet, the compressor looks for a Rule whose Field Descriptors match all and only the header fields present, checking FID, then DI, then FP, then comparing values to the TV with the MO. If several Rules are valid, which one to use is left to the implementation. If none is valid, the packet is sent uncompressed under the dedicated RuleID, and the whole header is the residue.

The residues of all fields are concatenated in Rule order. For a variable-length field the residue is preceded by its size, encoded on 4 bits for sizes 0 to 14, as 0b1111 plus 8 bits for sizes 15 to 254, and as 0xfff plus 16 bits for larger sizes. A SCHC parser is assumed to sit alongside SCHC to identify fields; the Rules only say what to do with them.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule is a checklist for each part of the header: what value we expect, how to check it, and what to send. If a packet matches a checklist, we just send the checklist number and any bits that changed.

sections.title: Matching Operators and Actions
sections.content:
Four Matching Operators are defined: equal, ignore (always true), MSB(x) (the leftmost x bits equal the TV) and match-mapping (the value is in a list in the TV, identified by an index).

The Compression/Decompression Actions say what to send and how the receiver rebuilds the field. not-sent sends nothing and the decompressor uses the TV, and it SHOULD be used with equal because pairing it with ignore risks a decompressed value that differs from the original. value-sent sends the field in full and is generally used with ignore. mapping-sent sends the index, with the first list element at index 0. LSB sends only the least significant bits and the decompressor concatenates the TV's most significant bits with the received value. DevIID and AppIID rebuild an interface identifier from the L2 address. compute-* elides a field that can be recomputed, such as a length, and it must be applied after the CDAs of all the fields it depends on.
sections.plainLanguage: If the other side already knows a value, do not send it. If only a little of it changes, send just that little bit. If it can be worked out from other parts, do not send it at all.

sections.title: Fragmentation Messages and Tiles
sections.content:
When the SCHC Packet is too big for the link, SCHC F/R cuts it into tiles. Tiles MUST be non-empty and pairwise disjoint, and their union MUST equal the SCHC Packet. Some modes group tiles into numbered windows of WINDOW_SIZE tiles; tile indices count down from WINDOW_SIZE - 1 to 0 within each window. A Bitmap has one bit per tile of a window, where 1 means the tile arrived correctly.

Five messages exist: SCHC Fragment, SCHC ACK, SCHC ACK REQ, SCHC Sender-Abort and SCHC Receiver-Abort. Their header fields are the RuleID (in every message), the Datagram Tag DTag (size T bits, to tell apart packets in flight under the same RuleID), the window field W (size M bits), the Fragment Compressed Number FCN (size N bits), the Reassembly Check Sequence RCS (size U bits, only in All-1 fragments) and the 1-bit integrity-check flag C.

Two FCN values are special. All ones, All-1, marks the very last tile of the SCHC Packet. All zeros, All-0, marks the last tile of a window that is not the last one. A Regular SCHC Fragment MUST NOT have an all-ones FCN.

Integrity is checked at the receiver with the RCS. Using a CRC32 with polynomial 0xEDB88320 is RECOMMENDED as the default. The RCS is computed over the full SCHC Packet plus the padding bits of the fragment carrying the last tile. A SCHC ACK with C=1 reports success and carries no Bitmap. With C=0 and windows in use it carries a Compressed Bitmap, from which trailing 1 bits are dropped so the message ends on an L2 Word boundary. A Receiver-Abort looks like an ACK with C=1 followed by ones up to the next L2 Word boundary and one more L2 Word of ones, a pattern that never occurs in a legitimate ACK. Sender-Abort and Receiver-Abort MUST NOT be acknowledged.
sections.plainLanguage: A big message is cut into pieces, like a jigsaw puzzle sent in several envelopes. Each envelope says which piece it holds. At the end the receiver counts a special check number to make sure the puzzle was put together right.

sections.title: The Three Fragmentation Modes
sections.content:
All SCHC Fragments of one SCHC Packet MUST use the same mode. The RFC does not say which modes a given LPWAN must implement; Profiles do.

No-ACK assumes out-of-sequence delivery does not occur and supports links with a variable MTU. Nothing flows back, so a unidirectional link is fine. Windows and the W field are not used. Each fragment carries exactly one tile, in order, and the last is an All-1 fragment. The receiver runs an Inactivity Timer per RuleID and DTag pair and drops the packet if integrity checking fails or the timer expires. A value of 1 is RECOMMENDED for N.

ACK-Always uses windows, with W of exactly 1 bit, and needs a feedback path. After a blind transmission of all tiles of a window, the sender waits for a SCHC ACK, retransmits any tiles reported missing, and moves to the next window only when the current one is complete. This gives a per-window lock-step. If the Retransmission Timer expires, the sender sends a SCHC ACK REQ until Attempts reaches MAX_ACK_REQUESTS, then sends a Sender-Abort.

ACK-on-Error supports variable MTU and out-of-order delivery and also needs a feedback path. W is wide enough to carry an absolute window number. A fragment may carry several contiguous tiles. The receiver sends an ACK only for windows that have missing tiles, and the sender may advance to later windows before earlier ones are confirmed. Transmission ends when integrity is confirmed, when too many attempts were made, or when the receiver sees too long an inactivity.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to send the pieces. One is shouting them and hoping. Another is checking after every small batch. The last is only speaking up when something is missing.

sections.title: Compressing IPv6 and UDP Headers
sections.content:
Section 10 shows how to write Rules for each IPv6 and UDP field. The patterns follow what is constant, what varies a little and what varies freely.

  • IPv6 Version: TV 6, MO ignore, CDA not-sent.
  • Traffic Class and Flow Label: if known and fixed (a Flow Label of zero, say), use equal and not-sent. If pseudorandom, use ignore and value-sent.
  • Payload Length and UDP Length: ignore with compute-*, so the decompressor recomputes them.
  • Hop Limit: in Uplink it is elided with a known constant. In Downlink it is forced to 1 at the receiver, which prevents any further forwarding.
  • Addresses: each is split into a 64-bit prefix and a 64-bit IID, identified by role (Dev or App) rather than by source or destination. A prefix can be not-sent or sent as a mapping-sent index, and an IID derived from the L2 address uses DevIID or AppIID.
  • UDP ports: elided when both ends know them, sent as LSB if only a few bits vary, or sent in full.

The UDP checksum is normally sent. A SCHC compressor MAY elide it when another layer gives at least equal integrity protection. For example, a fragmentation RCS of 2 bytes or more provides equal or better protection, under the conditions listed in the RFC. The RFC gives no recommendations for IPv6 extension headers.

Appendix A has a worked set of Rules in which Rule 0 tags uncompressed packets, and Rule 3 compresses each UDP port to 4 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of a header is the same every time, like the return address on all your letters. So you leave it out and only write down the bits that change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC expects SCHC to run on top of LPWAN technologies that have their own security measures, and it analyses what SCHC itself could add.

For compression, a forged SCHC Packet with an unknown RuleID should be silently dropped. With a valid RuleID, the reconstructed packet is at most a constant number of bits bigger than the received one, so decompression does not amplify attacks beyond a bounded amount. As a safety measure a decompressor should never rebuild a packet larger than MAX_PACKET_SIZE, with 1500 bytes as the generic default in a Profile. Because SCHC compresses field by field, compressed size does not leak correlations the way BREACH and CRIME do. Secret fields should still be sent with the same residue size regardless of their value, for example with ignore and value-sent. Using FP=0 or pairing ignore with not-sent can make the decompressed packet differ from the original.

For fragmentation, the RFC describes a buffer reservation attack, a corrupt fragment attack (a single spoofed ACK with all Bitmap bits at 0 triggers the repetition of WINDOW_SIZE tiles), and fragmentation as a way to bypass network inspection. It argues the last is not expected to apply because SCHC F/R is used over one LPWAN link. It also discusses a privacy concern around a predictable DTag, which it argues is not visible over the Internet assuming the tunnel provides confidentiality. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Because both sides share the same codebook, a faker cannot make a message blow up into something huge. The main worry is someone sending fake puzzle pieces to waste a tiny device's battery.
